extracted.intended_audience: educated public / political thinkers / legislators (readers of political philosophy and commentary)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for judging forms of government, representation, and revolutionary action as argued in a political-essay context (reflections on the French Revolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification for government: virtue and wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: No qualification for government but virtue and wisdom, actual or presumptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power, authority, and distinction should not be confined to blood and titles; wherever virtue and wisdom (actual or presumptive) are found they are the passport to place and honor. The road to eminence ought not to be made too easy; rare merit should pass through some sort of probation. The 'temple of honor' should be seated on an eminence—virtue is tried by difficulty and struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must show ability as well as property
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is a due and adequate representation of a state that does not represent its ability as well as its property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability is vigorous and active while property is sluggish; unless property is predominant in representation it cannot be safely protected. Representation should therefore give preponderance to ability and protect property in great masses to serve as a natural rampart around lesser properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetuation of property and hereditary security
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of perpetuating our property in our families is one of the most valuable and interesting circumstances belonging to it, and that which tends the most to the perpetuation of society itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hereditary property and hereditary distinction form natural securities for transmission; institutions like a House of Peers founded on hereditary property act as ballast for the commonwealth. Large proprietors, even if not perfect, stabilize society and protect lesser properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against leveling: some social descriptions must be uppermost
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who attempt to level, never equalize. In all societies, consisting of various descriptions of citizens, some description must be uppermost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leveling perverts the natural order by setting up in the air what should be on the ground. Associations of artisans cannot be equal to the situation required for high office; permitting low or servile occupations to rule causes the state to suffer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not every occupation is a matter of honor
rubrics_metrics.description: If he meant only that no honest employment was disgraceful...in asserting that anything is honorable, we imply some distinction in its favor. The occupation of a hairdresser or of a working tallow-chandler cannot be a matter of honor to any person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While honest employments should not suffer oppression from the state, the state suffers if such occupations (individually or collectively) are permitted to rule. Assertions that all occupations are equally honorable are politically dangerous when used to justify leveling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid election by lot or rotation (sortition)
rubrics_metrics.description: No rotation; no appointment by lot; no mode of election operating in the spirit of sortition or rotation can be generally good in a government conversant in extensive objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such modes have no tendency to select the man with a view to the duty or to accommodate person to office. Rare merit should not be made too easy to obtain; selection requires some probation and deliberate mechanism to match duties with persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government and constitution-making are practical sciences requiring experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of constructing a commonwealth... is not to be taught a priori... it requires experience, and even more experience than any person can gain in his whole life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One should exercise infinite caution before pulling down institutions that have served tolerably well for ages; reform should be guided by models and patterns of approved utility because immediate effects may mislead and remote effects may differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights in civil society are conventions and must be limited
rubrics_metrics.description: If civil society be the offspring of convention, that convention must be its law... how can any man claim under the conventions of civil society rights which do not so much as suppose its existence?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural rights in the abstract may be perfect in theory but impractical; civil society requires surrendering some natural rights (e.g., judging one's own cause) to obtain justice and order. Rights that are repugnant to the conventions of civil society cannot be exercised within it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must restrain passions as part of securing rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Among these wants is... a sufficient restraint upon their passions... the inclinations of men should frequently be thwarted, their will controlled, and their passions brought into subjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restraints on men are as much part of their rights as liberties: civil institutions exist to provide the wisdom and mechanisms for restraining passions so society can function. Policy should call in practical expertise (farmers, physicians) rather than metaphysical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex mixed constitutions preferred to simple systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple governments are fundamentally defective... It is better that the whole should be imperfectly and anomalously answered than that, while some parts are provided for with great exactness, others might be totally neglected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity may answer a single end well but fails to meet the complex and varied ends of society. Designers of constitutions who prize simplicity risk neglecting important facets of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of men (theorists) are extremes and must be moderated
rubrics_metrics.description: The pretended rights of these theorists are all extremes; and in proportion as they are metaphysically true, they are morally and politically false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political reason requires balancing, weighing, and compromise; rights in government are advantages that must be computed morally (adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing) rather than accepted as absolute metaphysical truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish right from power; power does not equal legitimate right
rubrics_metrics.description: By these theorists the right of the people is almost always sophistically confounded with their power... The body of the community, whenever it can come to act, can meet with no effectual resistance; but till power and right are the same, the whole body of them has no right inconsistent with virtue, and the first of all virtues, prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popular power does not automatically confer legitimate right in matters inconsistent with prudence or the public good. Claims to rights must be reasonable and beneficial, not merely expressions of raw power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid habitual revolutionary rhetoric and periodic calls to resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: This distemper of remedy, grown habitual, relaxes and wears out, by a vulgar and prostituted use, the spring of that spirit which is to be exerted on great occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making revolution or resistance a regular theme (anniversary sermons, constant talk of revolt) cheapens the principle, exhausts readiness to act on truly extreme occasions, and leads some theorists to hypocrisy or practical inaction when moderation would be wiser.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of representation is a practical, not merely formal, question
rubrics_metrics.description: I state here the doctrine of the Revolutionists only that you and others may see what an opinion these gentlemen entertain of the constitution of their country... our representation has been found perfectly adequate to all the purposes for which a representation of the people can be desired or devised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Charges of 'inadequate representation' should be tested against the practical purposes representation is meant to serve, not abstract criteria of numerical equality. Practical functioning and historical success matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: National governability requires unified structures; excessive fragmentation is destabilizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Do you seriously think that the territory of France, upon the republican system of eighty-three independent municipalities... can ever be governed as one body?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A constitution that effectively dismembers a nation into many small republics risks losing the capacity to act as a unified body; central organs (a capital, cohesive institutions) are necessary for united action and to prevent local monopolies of spoils or power.
